The trick is matching payroll to our actual traffic patterns, so I'm not overstaffed on slow days and scrambling on busy ones. I look at our peak hours—we get crushed on Friday and Saturday nights and Sunday mornings—so that's where I schedule my strongest people. I also build flexibility in; I cross-train associates so I'm not locked into one person per department. I run a tight budget, but I make sure I'm never sacrificing the customer experience or burning people out with back-to-back closing shifts.

answers.q: Walk me through what you do during a typical Friday or Saturday dinner service at Magnolia Bistro.
answers.answer: So we're doing 250 covers on those nights, and I'm running sauté and grill. My job is to keep my tickets moving—I hold myself to under 14 minutes on my stations no matter how deep the tickets get. I'm prepping my mise en place at the start, staying organized during service, communicating with the expo about what's timing, and then after service I break down my station completely, label and date everything for the next day, and make sure we're good on food safety. It's about being ready, staying calm under pressure, and making sure every plate that goes out is right.

answers.q: Tell me about training those three new cooks on sauté. What's your approach?
answers.answer: I've trained three new line cooks on sauté station and I take it seriously because sauté is one of the most important stations—it's about heat control and timing. My approach is showing them the steps hands-on, letting them watch me do it a few times, then getting them on the station with me right there so they can ask questions. I make sure they understand our plating guide so every plate looks the same. I also tell them it's okay to mess up in training—that's when you learn. Once they're ready I step back but stay close, and we keep building from there.
answers.resume_fact: Trained 3 new line cooks on the sauté station and our plating guide

answers.q: You mentioned cutting produce waste by about a third at Crescent Catering. How did you do that?
answers.answer: I was running the walk-in rotation at the catering company, and I noticed we were losing a lot of product just sitting around. So I started really paying attention to what was already in there before we prepped new stuff, using older product first, and being more precise with my cuts so we weren't throwing trim away unnecessarily. I also communicated with the other cooks about what we actually needed so we weren't over-prepping. It wasn't rocket science, just being mindful and not letting things get lost in the back. Cutting waste by about a third meant better food cost and less money down the drain.
answers.resume_fact: Ran the walk-in rotation and cut weekly produce waste by about a third

answers.q: What's your experience with food safety and what does passing every health inspection mean to you?
answers.answer: I got my ServSafe cert in 2024 and I take food safety seriously because it's not just about rules—it's about respect for the people eating. At Magnolia Bistro we've passed every health inspection since I started, and that's because I'm labeling and dating everything, rotating stock properly, keeping my station clean, and making sure temperatures are right. When I prep and break down I do it the right way every single time, not just when I know an inspector's coming. It's a habit. You cut corners on food safety and you're putting people at risk, so that's just not an option.
